questions.prompt: You shut a VM down from inside its operating system. What happens to compute billing?

options.text: You keep paying for compute because the VM is still allocated
The VM and its disks are permanently deleted

questions.explanation: An in-OS shutdown leaves the VM allocated, so compute keeps billing. Only deallocating (portal Stop or `az vm deallocate`) releases the compute.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Azure VMs are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: You choose an image (OS) and a size (CPU/memory) when creating one
SSH keys are more secure than passwords for Linux VMs
Managed disks are billed even while the VM is deallocated
Exposing SSH/RDP to the whole internet is a recommended default

questions.explanation: You pick image and size; SSH keys beat passwords; disks cost while deallocated. Exposing SSH/RDP to the entire internet is a security risk to avoid.

questions.prompt: Releasing a VM's compute so you stop paying for its vCPUs (while keeping the disks) is called ____.
questions.explanation: Deallocating releases the compute so you stop paying for vCPUs; disks and static IPs still cost until you delete them.

questions.prompt: Order the typical lifecycle of a learning VM.
questions.explanation: Create, connect and use, deallocate to pause billing, then delete the resource group to remove everything.

questions.prompt: Match each VM concept to its meaning.

pairs.right: The OS/software template a VM starts from
The VM's CPU and memory configuration
An Azure-managed virtual disk backing the VM
How you connect to a Linux VM

questions.explanation: Image = the OS template; size = CPU/memory; managed disk = the VM's storage; SSH = remote connection for Linux.
